title: Savitribai and Jyotirao Phule Open a School for Girls
text:
Jyotirao Phule was born in 1827 in Pune into a family of the Mali caste, gardeners, who were low in the caste hierarchy. He was married at thirteen to Savitribai, who was about nine and could not read. Jyotirao taught her at home, and she then trained as a teacher.

In 1848 the couple opened a school for girls in Pune, in a house called Bhide Wada. It was one of the first schools for girls run by Indians, and Savitribai became its teacher, perhaps the first woman teacher of her kind in India. They also opened their classes to children of the castes considered untouchable.

Many in the city were outraged. According to accounts handed down about her, as Savitribai walked to school people insulted her and threw mud, dung and stones at her. She carried a second sari in her bag and changed when she arrived. Under pressure from the community, Jyotirao's father made the couple leave the family home. They kept going. By the early 1850s they were running several schools.

The couple went on together to fight caste discrimination and child marriage, opened a home for widows and their infants, and adopted a widow's son. Jyotirao died in 1890. Savitribai, a poet as well as a teacher, died in 1897 of plague, caught while caring for patients during an epidemic.
lesson: A husband and wife united by a cause can face down a whole society. Sharing knowledge with the people closest to us can be the start of a revolution.
source: Rosalind O'Hanlon, Caste, Conflict and Ideology (1985); Jyotirao Phule's writings
caveat: Some details, such as the stones and the second sari, come from later biographies and tradition.
